chapter_theme: The nature of love (காமநுதலியல்): love needs both union and the sulking that interrupts it, and its pain is separation, felt most at evening and in the rains. The chapter ends with a girl's flight with her lover, seen by her mother and herself, and a woman's grief at a lover gone to seek wealth.
structure_note: Nearly every quatrain is dramatised speech in the manner of akam poetry, and Mudaliar names the speaker and situation for most: the woman, her friend, the returning man, the lover praising her eyes, and the mother. 391 states a principle; 392-394 and 397 are separation at evening or in the rain; 396, 398 and 399 concern the elopement; 400 is separation for wealth.

391.reading: Lord of the cool shore with long backwaters where the bright sea's restless waves beat: without embrace, pallor spreads; without sulking and pining, love has no salt; embracing and then sulking is one way.
391.nuance: Mudaliar takes உப்பு as sweetness and compares the Sanskrit theorists, who call separation the sweeter mode. The verse sets pallor and saltlessness as twin dangers: love needs both union and its interruption.

392.reading: For women without the companion whose garlanded chest they would embrace till it swelled, the clouds thundering in every direction as the rain comes down sound like the beat of a funeral drum.
392.nuance: The verse doesn't say why the rain hurts. Mudaliar does: the man promised to come back by the rainy season, so the rains arriving without him are the sign of a broken word.

393.reading: In the bewildering evening, when craftsmen have put away their tools, she was choosing flowers and weaving a garland; she threw down the garland in her hand and wept: 'What use is this garland to those without a companion?'
393.nuance: The verse ends on இம்மாலை, which can mean 'this garland' or 'this evening'. The commentators take it as the garland, but the double sense may be intended. Mudaliar has the friend report the scene to the man.

394.reading: Watching the setting sun, flicking away again and again with soft fingers the tears in her red-streaked eyes, sobbing, does she, alas, count the days on her soft fingers and reckon up my faults, lying on the bed with her arm for a pillow?
394.nuance: Mudaliar has the man speak this to his charioteer on the way home, imagining her grief, and cites Kural 1261. 'Our faults' turns her counting of days into a reckoning of his wrongs.

395.reading: Taking my beloved's eyes for carp, the little kingfisher followed her; but though it followed and rose eager to strike, it didn't dive, recognising her bright brow as a drawn bow.
395.nuance: Mudaliar calls it மயக்கவணி, the figure of mistaken identity, and has the man say it in wonder to his friend. Pope adds that the man is showing his own timid reverence.

396.reading: Feet that drew back in fear, crying 'gently, gently', even when red dye was applied with soft cotton: have they, alas, borne the stony desert path, the feet of my girl with lily-scented lips and lovely waist?
396.nuance: Mudaliar identifies the speaker as the girl's mother, who has learned that her daughter has gone with her lover through the wilderness. The verse sets the softest touch the mother knows against the hardest ground she can imagine.

397.reading: In the dim red evening, when the palm-leaf accountants fall silent, she thought of the parting of the man who married her, tore off her garland, and wept, rubbing away the sandal paste that adorned her lovely breasts.
397.nuance: Mudaliar records two settings: the friend describing her grief in his absence, or the friend telling the man she won't consent to his going. The second makes the parting still to come. He also reports a view that the silenced voices are schoolchildren reciting, which Shanmuganar adopts.

398.reading: You ask, friend of the bright bangles, whether I can walk tomorrow behind my young bull of a man through the forest that is hard to cross; a man who gets a great horse learns to ride it that very moment.
398.nuance: The answer is a proverb: the ability comes with the thing. Mudaliar spells out the hint, that following one's husband is not hard. Pope's 'his enthusiasm teaches him' is his own explanation.

399.reading: I didn't understand the sign at all when she embraced me so that my nipples, my pearls and my whole body were pressed; it seems the sign my sweet doll made meant she was about to take the path where herds of deer flee from the tiger.
399.nuance: Mudaliar has the mother speak after her daughter's flight. The embrace was a farewell that only the leaving gave meaning to.

400.reading: The three-eyed one, the crow, the hooded snake, the mother who bore me: what wrong did they do? Friend with breasts like golden kongu buds, it is the road my lover took for wealth.
400.nuance: The verse names four suspects and acquits them without saying why. Both commentators supply the myths: Siva burned Kama and let him live again, the crow raised the koel's chick, the snake swallowed the moon and released it, and the mother let her live, so each lies behind one torment of separation. On that reading she refuses the easy targets and blames the one real cause, the journey for wealth. The verse closes the Naladiyar.

links.note: Both make sulking love's salt: 1302 measures it, with too much spoiling the dish, and 391 says love without it has no salt at all.
1306 says love without quarrels, serious and light, is like over-ripe or unripe fruit; 391 says that union and sulking together are love's way.
The good wife of 384 sulks at the right moment and relents sweetly; 391 gives the reason, that without sulking love has no salt.
In both, a sound of the season becomes a killing instrument for the separated woman: the rain's thunder is a funeral drum in 392, and the herdsman's flute a weapon in 1228.

The funeral drum appears in both: in 364 it should teach a man to give up married life, and in 392 the thunder sounds like it to a woman whose husband is away. The same sound serves renunciation in one book and love in the other.
Both make evening the bewildering hour of separation: 393's மம்மர்கொள் மாலை, and 1229's evening that confuses the mind of the whole town.
Two evening scenes in one frame: the day's work falls silent, and the woman casts off her garland and weeps for the absent man.
Both have the woman count the days of absence on her fingers, and Mudaliar cites 1261 with 394. In 1261 she speaks; in 394 the man imagines it.
Both make her brow a bow that guards her eyes: in 1086 the brows, if they would only screen her eyes, would spare him his pain, and in 395 they frighten off the kingfisher.
The mother of 396 doubts that feet which shrank from soft dye can bear the stony path; the girl of 398 answers that the strength comes with the man, as riding comes with the horse.
Both are the mother's speech after her daughter's flight: 396 fears for the girl's feet on the way, and 399 rereads the farewell embrace she didn't understand.

1225's woman asks what she did to morning and to evening, looking for the cause of her pain in the hours. 400 runs through such suspects and acquits them, blaming only the road her lover took for wealth.

new_concepts.gloss: a girl's going away with her lover, against her family, through the wilderness
new_concepts.label_source: Mine, the akam tradition's name for the situation; the verses don't use the word, and Mudaliar describes it as the man taking her with him (உடன் கொண்டுபோன).

source_issues: 394: Pope's translation is not aligned, and the Tamil reads சிதரா஢க்கண், a garbled character for சிதரரிக்கண் (Mudaliar: சிதர் அரி).
398: Shanmuganar's field also contains the text of 399 and his commentary on it, and 399 has no Shanmuganar commentary aligned.
399: the Tamil reads ஦வ்ருஉம், a garbled form of வெரூஉம் as Mudaliar glosses it; the printed verse has தீம்பாவை where Mudaliar and Shanmuganar's copy read பூம்பாவை.
400: Shanmuganar's field ends with his colophon and a closing verse in praise of the Naladiyar.
